historyReviewBoundary: All 115 histories have author source checks. Final independent review covered metadata and numerical checks for all 115 classes, 12 deeper class targets and source-gap samples in seven classes. It did not independently verify every passage of every cited source.

history.name: Antibacterial dihydrofolate-reductase inhibitors

starting.description: Known bacterial nutrient-growth requirements motivated the L. casei assay and studies of thymine-related bases. Synthetic base analogues then inhibited this model and pathogens; the team developed a diaminopyrimidine series and studied folate-dependent growth responses.

inspiration.description: Known nutrient-dependent bacterial growth informed the assay, with the natural nucleic-acid base thymine a reference for studying related structures; inhibition by synthetic base analogues and differential responses to folate forms informed subsequent development.

steps.description: Known folate, thymine and purine relationships in bacterial growth motivated the L. casei model and studies of thymine analogues; synthetic analogues inhibited that system and pathogenic bacteria.

Falco began a diaminopyrimidine series; the team observed folate-antagonist activity in L. casei and differential folic-versus-folinic-acid growth responses that supported a folate-reduction interpretation.

For antibacterial use, the team selected among 5-benzylpyrimidines for selectivity and other useful properties. They reported trimethoprim's stronger antibacterial action than earlier candidates and the absence of their particular side effects in monkeys.

In a 1965 enzyme study the group reported distinct species-specific inhibition patterns and a correlation between drug binding and suppression of the source organism. The available abstract does not identify which compounds were tested.
The group tested trimethoprim with sulfonamides in bacterial cultures and mouse infections, reporting potentiation in selected settings.

design.description: The group synthesized and screened base analogues, developed and selected 2,4-diaminopyrimidines with differential antimicrobial activity, selected trimethoprim for antibacterial properties and tolerability in the stated tests, and investigated sulfonamide combinations.

circumstances.description: The initial synthetic-analogue investigation and use of observed biological differences were deliberate. According to the 1993 review's abstract, substituted diaminopyrimidines' interference with folate utilization rather than the expected thymine antagonism was unexpected; the underlying original account for that expectation was not read.

limits: The antibacterial trimethoprim lineage is the assigned scope; methotrexate and the antimalarial pyrimethamine are contextual comparators, not cohort members.
conflicts: Hitchings's 1988 retrospective puts a conclusion about selective reductase inhibitors by 1950 (E13); Then's 1993 abstract dates identification of trimethoprim's specific reductase target to 1965 (E12). These may describe an earlier general inference and a later trimethoprim-specific identification, not necessarily conflicting events. The exact chronology and evidentiary basis remain unadjudicated.
gaps: The 1948 and 1952 early reports and the original 1962 antibacterial chemistry report were located but not read. The exact development decisions and priority for each substitution are not established here.
Only the abstract of the 1965 purified-enzyme study was read; that abstract does not name trimethoprim or determine the first date its target was established.
Then's 1993 review was available only as an abstract; the original evidence for its claimed initial expectation of thymine antagonism was not read.
